Q: How to make this stream gatherer threadsafe? A:

Your understanding is incorrect. You do not need to synchronize Holder. The Stream / Gatherer implementation does not lock get/set either. It never lets two threads mutate the same Holder at the same time. The combining thread may later read a Holder written by another thread. Visibility is provided by the stream implementation, not by Holder.That is why a parallel run still finds the max.

Parallel gatherers isolate state; they do not synchronize it

Gatherer.of(...) is parallelizable because you supplied a real combiner. On a parallel stream the pipeline does this:

  1. Split the source into partitions.

  2. Call the initializer once per partition. Each worker gets its own Holder.

  3. Run the integrator only against that partition's Holder.

  4. After both partitions finish integrating, call the combiner to merge the two holders.

  5. Call the finisher once on the final merged state.

The Gatherer javadoc requires that partitions are processed in isolation, combining happens only after integration is complete for both partitions, and once a state object is passed to the combiner or finisher it is never passed back to the integrator.

So thread A never calls set on thread B's Holder. Isolation is not the same as synchronization.

This is the same model as a non-concurrent Collector. Collectors.toList() uses a plain ArrayList on parallel streams for the same reason: each partition has its own list; the combiner concatenates them later.

Each thread computes a local max. The combiner then picks the larger of the two local maxes. That is ordinary parallel reduction, not a race on one shared box.

partition 1: Holder(12) + partition 2: Holder(99)

                      |

               combiner -\> Holder(99)

                      |

               finisher -\> push(99)

Why Holder looking "unsafe" does not matter

This would be a data race:

Holder<Integer> shared = new Holder<>();

Gatherer.of(() -> shared, ...); // every partition mutates the SAME object

Your initializer is:

() -> new Holder<Integer>()

Each partition gets a new instance. get/set are not concurrent on that instance, so adding synchronized would only add overhead.

parallel() after gather() still parallelizes the gatherer. The last parallel() / sequential() before the terminal operation sets the mode for the whole pipeline:

al.stream().gather(maxer).parallel().forEach(System.out::println);

// same evaluation mode as

al.parallelStream().gather(maxer).forEach(System.out::println);

So the gatherer is running in parallel. It still works because state is partition-local, not because the JDK locks Holder.

The real bugs

The gatherer is already thread-safe and still incorrect on some inputs.

The combiner NPEs on an empty partition:

(state1, state2) -> state1.get() > state2.get() ? state1 : state2

An empty split leaves Holder.t == null. The > operator unboxes Integer and throws NullPointerException.

Parallel splits of a 100,000-element ArrayList are usually non-empty, so this test hides the bug. Smaller lists, a filter, or an unlucky split can hit it.

The finisher on an empty stream:

(state, ds) -> ds.push(state.get());

If nothing was ever set, this pushes null.

The combiner is the only place two threads' results meet. It must treat "no value yet" as empty, not as a number.

Correct gatherer (still no locks)

Gatherer<Integer, Holder<Integer>, Integer> maxer = Gatherer.of(

    Holder::new,

    Gatherer.Integrator.ofGreedy((state, element, downstream) -\> {

        Integer current = state.get();

        if (current == null || current \< element) {

            state.set(element);

        }

        return true;

    }),

    (left, right) -\> {

        if (left.get() == null) return right;

        if (right.get() == null) return left;

        return left.get() \>= right.get() ? left : right;

    },

    (state, downstream) -\> {

        if (state.get() != null) {

            downstream.push(state.get());

        }

    }

);

al.parallelStream().gather(maxer).forEach(System.out::println);

Integrator.ofGreedy is appropriate here because you never short-circuit, so the implementation does not need to inspect false on every element.

Use Gatherer.of(...) when you have an associative combiner. Use Gatherer.ofSequential(...) only when the operation cannot be split (windows, running totals). Sequential gatherers use defaultCombiner() and stay sequential even if you call parallel().

When you would need thread safety

  • The initializer returns a shared object (static, captured local, singleton).

  • The integrator / combiner / finisher mutates some other shared field, list, or map.

  • You keep a Downstream or state reference and use it after the callback returns (the javadoc forbids that).

None of those apply to a per-partition Holder.

Bottom line: do not make this gatherer thread-safe by synchronizing Holder. The framework already confines each state object to one thread during integration. Your job is a combiner that merges two finished local maxes and handles empty partitions. The experiment "it found the max without synchronized, so either I am wrong or the JDK locks state" — you were wrong about sharing. The JDK isolates state; it does not lock it.

Q: Does C++ compile to assembly? A:

The vast majority of C++ compilers will convert the C++ source into object files (machine code with enough control information to be linked into an executable). They may actually generate assembly language as an interim step and even use a separate assembler for processing the assembler source, but you'll generally never see that. For example, you have to actually go out of your way to get gcc to generate assembly code (.s file) by using the -S flag. Normally, you would never see the assembly.

But the C++ standard doesn't mandate the final form that's output from the compiler, just that the code has to behave in a certain way when you run it.

In fact, the earliest C++ "compilers" (called CFRONT, presumably because it was a front end to C) actually generated C source code and then compiled that.

You can have your C++ compiler generate object code, Java byte code, or even GWBASIC, should you be feeling masochistic.
